title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry
description: An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025. Mike Blake | ReutersDETROIT — The automot
body: An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025. Mike Blake | ReutersDETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday. President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal."That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.Trump negotiated USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum."Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."Honda is the second-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor, but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants."I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

schema.headline: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry

title: Nvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership
description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNvidia
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNvidia and Advanced Micro Devices have said they will invest a total of $4 billion in Meta after the social media and artificial intelligence giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in AI infrastructure.Meta on Monday said it would initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.Nvidia on Tuesday said it would invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering, with AMD announcing it would invest $1 billion. Meta's Monday announcement said Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.Nvidia, AMD deepen Meta tiesNvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant's AI agent that launched last month."AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Technology Conference (GTC) on October 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Sean Gallup | Getty Images"This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents.""We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people," said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.AMD said that its Helios racks were running at Meta and its EPYC processors were powering Meta's Muse. "Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta's most ambitious superintelligence models and services," AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a statement.AMD was up 3% on Tuesday, while Nvidia stayed flat. Meta was down 1%.Nvidia and AMD have been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI and participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022. AMD in July said it would make an equity investment of up to $5 billion in Anthropic. The company has been involved in 25 funding rounds in 2026, up from just two in 2022.

schema.headline: Nvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership

title: Coca-Cola hikes earnings outlook, even as it sees lackluster demand in North America
description: Multipacks of Coca-Cola Original Taste glass bottles, 4x200ml, line a supermarket shelf in Bari, Italy, on September 15, 2026. Matteo Della Torre | Nu
body: Multipacks of Coca-Cola Original Taste glass bottles, 4x200ml, line a supermarket shelf in Bari, Italy, on September 15, 2026. Matteo Della Torre | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesCoca-Cola on Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market.For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth.CEO Henrique Braun attributed the company's strong results to its "speed and discipline" despite the "uneven environment," he said on the company's earnings conference call. Looking ahead to 2027, the company expects consumer behavior to remain unchanged, CFO John Murphy said. In recent quarters, Braun and other executives have said North American shoppers are under pressure, stretched thin by inflation and economic uncertainty, and looking for value. But the beverage giant has also said consumers are still buying its drinks, from premium brands like Fairlife to its namesake soda. Shares of the company fell less than 1% in morning trading on its gloomy forecast for the consumer environment.Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting: Earnings per share: 91 cents adjusted vs. 88 cents expectedRevenue: $13.4 billion vs. $12.92 billion expected Coke reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $4.01 billion, or 93 cents per share, up from $3.7 billion, or 86 cents per share, a year earlier.Excluding transaction gains and other items, Coke earned 91 cents per share.Net sales rose 7% to $13.4 billion. Coke's organic revenue, which strips out acquisitions, divestitures and foreign currency, also climbed 7% in the quarter.For the second straight quarter, the company's unit case volume increased 5%, helped by higher demand outside of North America. Coke's home market reported flat volume. However, the company's North American business would have reported volume growth if not for the timing of the Fourth of July holiday and the monthslong shortage of Topo Chico, a sparkling water brand Coke owns, Murphy told CNBC."The underlying momentum remains quite strong," he said. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."In North America, Coke's at-home business is faring better than its away-from-home segment, which includes restaurants, movie theaters and amusement parks. The restaurant industry is still under pressure, and Coke expects that to continue through the rest of the year, Murphy told analysts on the company's earnings conference call.Globally, Coke's sparkling soft drinks business saw volume increase 5% during the quarter, lifted by growth of Coke, Coke Zero Sugar and Diet Coke. Diet Coke is having a "resurgence," Murphy told CNBC. Gen Z consumers in the U.S. have nicknamed it a "fridge cigarette," while consumers in India threw Diet Coke parties as shortages tied to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran have made the drink scarce."It's a brand that's almost reinventing itself with the next generation of consumers," he said.Coke has also gained market share as rival PepsiCo sees its soda business struggle, according to Murphy. Still, some of Coke's soda brands, like Sprite, have "some work to do."Coke's water, sports, coffee and tea division also saw volume climb by 5%. Increased demand for its water, which includes its premium Smartwater brand, fueled the growth. Demand for its tea and coffee was flat, while sports drinks declined.The company's juice, value-added dairy and plant-based beverages business reported flat volume, despite growth in brands like Fairlife and Minute Maid.

schema.headline: Coca-Cola hikes earnings outlook, even as it sees lackluster demand in North America

title: Melania Trump-brokered local ceasefire begins as Russia continues attacks on Ukraine
description: As a ceasefire brokered by First Lady Melania Trump took effect in a city in southern Ukraine, Russia continued pounding Ukraine's cities overnight. T
body: As a ceasefire brokered by First Lady Melania Trump took effect in a city in southern Ukraine, Russia continued pounding Ukraine's cities overnight. The local ceasefire, due to last until Saturday in Russia-occupied Oleshky near the Crimean Peninsula, began at 3:00 a.m. local time to permit humanitarian aid to reach the city's inhabitants who are stranded amid shortages of food, water, and medicines. Oleshky, in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region, lies across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, about 340 miles southeast of Kyiv. Russian forces captured the town at the start of their 2022 invasionThe temporary Oleshky ceasefire came as Kyiv reported Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks targeting some of Ukraine's biggest cities overnight. As many as 16 ballistic missiles and 280 drones were launched by Russia, resulting in casualties, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said early Tuesday. "Almost everywhere, Russia's targets were the energy sector, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure," Zelenskyy said."Strikes are taking place every day. Russia is constantly taking new steps toward escalation."The developments come ahead of a new round of trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the U.S.Following a visit to Europe by U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff for separate talks with Zelenskyy and Putin, the leaders emphasized that they were open to negotiations, but security guarantees were essential.On Tuesday, Putin held talks with leaders of bordering countries, Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. In a phone call, Stubb and Støre emphasized to Putin that their countries would continue to support Ukraine and that negotiations to end the war must resume, according to the Norwegian government. The so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Oct. 11 appears to have failed to yield any meaningful outcome.A deal with the U.S. that will see Russia supply global markets with diesel, as well as recently reported restrictions on military applications of SpaceX's Starlink internet service, led Ukrainian officials to warn that Russia was emboldened to intensify attacks on civilian and energy targets.

schema.headline: Melania Trump-brokered local ceasefire begins as Russia continues attacks on Ukraine

title: Lula’s election win leaves Brazil facing a fiscal tightrope
description: Presidential candidate and incumbent president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of Brazil celebrates after the results of the general election day on October
body: Presidential candidate and incumbent president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of Brazil celebrates after the results of the general election day on October 25, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.Rodrigo Paiva | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva's surprise re-election as Brazil's president on Sunday prompted a sharp market reaction — and showed the tightrope he must walk between pleasing his grassroots base and nervous investors who could fuel a fiscal crisis.The country's benchmark stock index tumbled 13.9% on Monday, the sharpest daily decline since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Brazilian real fell nearly 8% against the U.S. dollar, the most since 1999.The yield on Brazil's 10-year government bond rose 2.46 percentage points to its highest level in more than a decade. The moves wiped out a rally in Brazilian assets that followed Flávio Bolsonaro, seen as the more market-friendly and fiscally disciplined of the candidates, winning the first-round vote in early October.Lula, who has been in office since Jan. 1, 2023 and was president before from 2003 to 2011, now faces a host of challenges, including a heavily right-wing Congress opposed to many of his policies and hostility from the White House.Slow growth, high inflation and ratesEconomic issues will be top of the pile. Growth is slowing in Latin America's biggest economy, and inflation and interest rates are high. Lula has promised expensive measures that appeal to his grassroots base. Those include protections of existing benefits, minimum-wage increases ahead of inflation, expansions of housing and education support programs, tax cuts on food essentials and a reduction in the country's long working week to 40 hours without pay cuts. His ability to deliver will "revolve around a central tension," Rafael Ch, senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, said in a note Tuesday.Voters want "tangible improvements in household finances," and the election result will be seen as an endorsement of higher social spending, Ch said.But bond markets are already uneasy with Brazil's growing debt-to-GDP ratio, and are likely to demand an ever-higher premium if public spending rises significantly. The Brazilian Treasury on Monday canceled two planned bond auctions scheduled for this week amid concerns over demand and soaring yields."Insufficiently funded fiscal expansion could leave the central bank cutting [interest rates] less, offsetting part of the relief Lula hopes to deliver," Ch said."We believe Lula will manage this tension through sequencing: reassure markets initially, capture the benefits of monetary easing, and subsequently seek greater fiscal flexibility to deliver his legacy agenda," he added.Reassurance will come through signals that he is preparing measures to increase the 2027 primary surplus, including a possible constitutional amendment expanding spending freezes, and appointing a market-conscious finance minister, Ch added.A key question will be whether markets view any fiscal discipline as temporary and whether Lula embarks on a spending spree ahead of the 2030 elections if support for the left falls, Ch said. "Even a limited easing cycle could weaken his commitment to restraint once some of its economic benefits have materialized," he said.Lula is facing a potential fiscal crisis "largely of his own making," Elizabeth Johnson, managing director of Brazil research at TS Lombard, said on Tuesday.Johnson also said that market-calming measures should be expected, including the curbing of civil-service benefits, reducing subsidized credit and the presentation of a proposal for a new "sin tax" — on goods such as alcohol and cigarettes — in the coming days.Meanwhile, the president will rush to approve reforms before the new legislature convenes in February, Johnson said, which "hinges on Lula's willingness to cut spending.""Our base case is that Lula will advance a modest fiscal reform, helping avert a major fiscal crisis in 2027," Johnson said. In the short term, Brazilian stocks would nonetheless suffer, according to Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell."Who will foot the bill for Lula's proposed welfare spending and debt moratorium for small enterprises remains to be seen, but the 10-year bond yield is likely to rise first and ask questions later, a development that can only serve to make Brazilian equities relatively less attractive," Mould said in a Tuesday note. Brazil's Ibovespa had been the best-performing major stock market index this year, he said, buoyed by Bolsonaro's expected victory and the country benefiting from higher commodity prices. The latest decline "in turn may not help wider pan-Latin American indices, which investors can easily access via exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The MSCI Latin America index hit a 12-year high this year, helped by the political rightward swing, which Brazil had been expected to join," Mould said.

schema.headline: Lula’s election win leaves Brazil facing a fiscal tightrope

title: Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar
description: Ripple and RobinhoodGetty ImagesRipple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and fi
body: Ripple and RobinhoodGetty ImagesRipple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients."Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."WorkhorseStablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash. "Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution.""This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline. Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.

schema.headline: Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

title: One week out, prediction markets see Democrats as favored to sweep Congress
description: The U.S. Capitol building is seen on March 27, 2026 in Washington, DC.Samuel Corum | Getty ImagesThe 2026 U.S. midterm election will be held a week fr
body: The U.S. Capitol building is seen on March 27, 2026 in Washington, DC.Samuel Corum | Getty ImagesThe 2026 U.S. midterm election will be held a week from Tuesday, with the Republican Party looking to defend majorities in both the House and Senate, though Democrats are seen as two-to-one favorites to flip both chambers blue on prediction markets. Speculators on platform Kalshi place a 63% chance that Democrats win control of both the House and Senate. Those odds have stayed relatively stable since the beginning of October. Meanwhile, there's just under a 10% chance that Republicans sweep both chambers, and a 29% chance Democrats win the House while the GOP maintains its majority in the Senate. Contracts on the market are resolved using official data from the U.S. Congress. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.On Sunday, prediction markets gave high odds to right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro to win in the Brazil presidential election before polls closed, though the incumbent left-wing president Lula da Silva was re-elected. Some markets in Democratic primaries this election cycle also drew criticism for giving sky-high odds to some candidates winning who ultimately only narrowly won or lost. Platforms, however, say that odds traders place often end up happening that exact percentage of the time. That means, essentially, that a candidate with a 20% chance to win on an event contract exchange pulls out an "upset" win 20% of the time. Before early September, Democrats had less than a 50% chance to sweep both chambers of Congress, though their odds have risen from around 30% earlier in the year before the start of the U.S.-Iran war and higher gas prices that have hit consumers. On Polymarket, Democrats have a 65% chance to sweep both houses. Polls broadly show Democrats favored in the national popular vote for the House, and competitive in a series of red-state Senate races that will decide control of the upper chamber. Though House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has cast doubt on those findings. "We've been from coast to coast," he said in an appearance on Fox News Monday, "and I'm telling you, the polling is inaccurate."Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: One week out, prediction markets see Democrats as favored to sweep Congress

title: World Bank's Banga: Availability of capital 'not really an issue' as AI demand drives up borrowing costs
description: watch nowWorld Bank President Ajay Banga said on Tuesday that capital remained available despite concerns of artificial intelligence sending interest
body: watch nowWorld Bank President Ajay Banga said on Tuesday that capital remained available despite concerns of artificial intelligence sending interest rates higher."It's not really an issue," Banga said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box."Banga said the World Bank mobilized $112 billion last year, around three times the amount recorded three years prior.He said investors may be concerned about circular financing and the business model tied to AI.But Banga told CNBC that emerging markets are not running into the same hesitancy because the investments focus more on infrastructure like bridges and roads.These countries also look at smaller-scale uses of AI, according to Banga. Banga said developed counterparts look to funding to support large use cases, which he described as the "exact opposite" need.The World Bank leader also said that the private capital it oversees does not go to governments. As a result, the organization can avoid fears of looming debt crises and challenges related to rising bond yields within some countries."In general, I still believe that AI is going to be transformative and profitable," Banga said. "But everybody sees bumps in the road from here to there, and no one knows when the next bump will come."Banga's comments come ahead of a string of interest rate decisions from central banks around the world. Economists and monetary policymakers across the globe have been attempting to gauge how the widespread adoption of AI impacts demand for capital and employment. The financial institution, which was founded in 1944, aims to end poverty and support economic prosperity through global partnerships and funding. Before taking the top job at the bank, Banga was vice chair at General Atlantic and CEO of Mastercard.

schema.headline: World Bank's Banga: Availability of capital 'not really an issue' as AI demand drives up borrowing costs

title: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
description: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn ext
body: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters, according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems."While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a press conference, amid the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, in Jerusalem, March 19, 2026. Ronen Zvulun | ReutersIn Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win. Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.25 October 2026, Israel, Tel Aviv: Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot addresses attendees from behind a lectern emblazoned with party slogans during an election rally. Erik Marmor | Picture Alliance | Getty Images"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system. While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting. Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats. "Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot." Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week. What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

schema.headline: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote

title: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup
description: Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software ma
body: Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable.Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it."OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET.For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic, filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering.Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27th, 2026.CNBCThiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits."More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release.Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip."Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said.It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs.Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers like OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large.OpenAI's Jalapeno chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said.Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday.Read more CNBC tech newsA guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectusNvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnershipApple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phoneAnthropic's IPO plans: 900% revenue retention, but $80 billion in first-half lossesThe announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloud Amazon Web Services announced plans to bring Cerebras hardware into its data centers, a major point of validation.Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company."We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said.A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule.Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital.Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting.Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline.—CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this articleStock Chart IconStock chart iconOracle stock chart.

schema.headline: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup

title: Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China
description: Michael Leiters, CEO of the Stuttgart-based sports car manufacturer Porsche, stands next to a Porsche 911 GT3 SC at the Porsche Development Center.Ber
body: Michael Leiters, CEO of the Stuttgart-based sports car manufacturer Porsche, stands next to a Porsche 911 GT3 SC at the Porsche Development Center.Bernd Weißbrod | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesGerman sports carmaker Porsche said it has significantly reduced its exposure to China as operating profit rebounded in the first nine months of the year despite falling revenue and vehicle deliveries.The Volkswagen-owned company published its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, announcing that operating profit was 1.74 billion euros ($1.94 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 40 million euros at the same time last year, when it booked around 2.7 billion euros in strategic restructuring costs.Meanwhile, sales revenue fell 5.9% to 25.28 billion euros, while deliveries continued to decline, down 16% to 178,532. North America remained Porsche's largest sales region by volume.China has historically been an important market for German luxury automakers, but they have struggled with growing competition from domestic brands, particularly in electric vehicles.Porsche's China sales have fallen sharply in recent years amid intensifying competition from brands such as BYD, Geely and Xiaomi."Our geographically balanced sales footprint continues to provide resilience across different markets," Jochen Breckner, Porsche's chief financial officer, said in the earnings webcast on Tuesday."As you know, we have significantly reduced our exposure to China. This makes our overall business less dependent on developments from this challenging market environment." Porsche shares were last seen trading 2.3% higher.Porsche is also cutting thousands of jobs as part of a broader restructuring aimed at reducing costs and responding to weaker demand.Citi: Porsche's underlying profit outpaces German luxury peersCiti analysts said in a note Tuesday that Porsche's first-nine-month results were as expected, despite challenges including China."Despite challenging conditions, including exceptionally low deliveries, higher costs, and higher battery electric vehicle deliveries, Porsche's underlying EBIT remains very resilient and ahead of German premium peers," the analysts said.They added that Porsche has laid out a plan to return to double-digit underlying operating profit margins, with recovery expected to start in 2028, and net cash flow expected to rebound to above its IPO levels by 2031. "Whilst FY27 will remain a trough year, we still see a solid, well-supported and credible multi-year EBIT and net cash recovery starting financial year 2028 - unlike many peers," the analysts said.

schema.headline: Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China

title: UPS beats quarterly expectations, raises full-year guidance again
description: A UPS delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on July 28, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesUnited Parcel Service on Tue
body: A UPS delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on July 28, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesUnited Parcel Service on Tuesday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year guidance.The guidance raise comes after the company already upped its outlook last quarter. UPS now said it's projecting full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion, as well as fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion. Shares of UPS rose slightly in morning trading. Here's how the company performed in its third quarter, compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $1.69 adjusted vs. $1.63 expectedRevenue: $22.9 billion vs. $22.29 billion expectedFor the quarter ended Sept. 30, UPS reported net income of $1.16 billion, or $1.37 per share, down slightly from net income of $1.31 billion, or $1.55, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time expenses, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.69. Revenue rose 6.7% to $22.9 billion.In its domestic segment, the company said it saw a 4.5% increase in revenue, while its international segment had a 7.1% rise in revenue. Its supply chain solutions business saw an 18.2% revenue increase, which UPS said was primarily driven to growth in forwarding and logistics, including healthcare. On a call with analysts, CEO Carol Tomé said healthcare revenue exceeded $3 billion for the third consecutive quarter. The company had previously said it expected its third-quarter domestic revenue to be flat and for domestic average daily volume to fall due to seasonal declines and the glide down with Amazon. "We're driving more premium growth, improving revenue quality and mix, and creating greater operating leverage through a more efficient network," Tomé said on the call. "All of this is strengthening the underlying performance of our business."UPS has been in the midst of a turnaround under Tomé's leadership, working to create a leaner business model and leveraging automation to position the company for growth. As the company prepares for its peak holiday season, Tomé said the consumer remains resilient, and the growth in average daily volume between the third and fourth quarters will be consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume is expected to fall due to the reduction with Amazon.She added that nearly 70% of all packages will flow through an automated process this holiday season.

schema.headline: UPS beats quarterly expectations, raises full-year guidance again

title: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes
description: FAIRFORD, ENGLAND - JULY 25: A B1 Bomber at RAF Fairford on July 25, 2026 in Fairford, England. (Photo by Matthew Horwood/Getty Images)Matthew Horwood
body: FAIRFORD, ENGLAND - JULY 25: A B1 Bomber at RAF Fairford on July 25, 2026 in Fairford, England. (Photo by Matthew Horwood/Getty Images)Matthew Horwood | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe U.K. has said it had charged a man with an offense of assisting a "foreign intelligence service" over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran.British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, has been charged under the country's National Security Act "following an incident involving RAF Fairford," an air base in west England, prosecutors announced on Tuesday. The Crown Prosecution Service said that, between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28, Abdulkarim is alleged to have engaged in "conduct that would likely materially assist a foreign intelligence service.""We believe that country to be Iran," the U.K.'s head of national counter-terrorism policing, Laurence Taylor, said in a statement.Prosecutors also charged 24-year-old Nouman Essghir with "entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK".The men appeared in court in London on Tuesday morning."We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state," Taylor added.He added that five other men arrested in connection with the investigation remain on police bail."While some of the circumstances remain unclear, we are confident that this activity was conducted on behalf of a foreign intelligence service," he said at a press conference later in the day. "This is not a theoretical threat," he added. "This is something we're responding to every day at counter-terrorism policing, particularly in the case of Iran."RAF Fairford's role in U.S. strikes on IranFive people were initially arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses near RAF Fairford on Sept. 28. Abdulkarim was interviewed and charged after some re-arrests were made earlier this month, investigators said on Tuesday. RAF Fairford had been used as the U.S. Air Force's command outpost for operations from Europe and for American strikes on Iranian missile sites.Announcing the charges made on Tuesday, Frank Ferguson, a chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said that they followed "a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford.""We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues," he said.After the initial arrests in September, U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. had moved its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to a threat "linked to Iran."Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers earlier this month that the incident was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."Over the summer, Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned it saw any military base involved in launching airstrikes on Iran as a legitimate target.Tehran denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

schema.headline: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes

title: Anthropic's IPO is risky business
description: CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as U.S. President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial inte
body: CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as U.S. President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAnthropic's much-anticipated initial public offering is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.More than 90 pages of Anthropic's IPO prospectus, revealed Monday, center on the AI lab's multitude of corporate risk factors, many of which go beyond the kinds of boilerplate scenarios typically found in  corporate filings.From the end of humanity to the company's current clash with the Trump administration, Anthropic's IPO document underscores how one of the most well-capitalized startups in history foresees the future of its operations.Anthropic's IPO gets existentialThe Claude maker's risks include a laundry list of ways its models can cause harm, including potentially  "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." It's imperative for Anthropic to emphasize AI safety because failure to do so could adversely affect its "brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations," the filing said. But fierce competition, market pressure and stakeholder expectations make the task of safely developing and implementing bleeding-edge foundation models particularly challenging.Anthropic can't guarantee that its AI safety efforts will be adequate, as the technology's inherent complexity makes it difficult for the company to plan for and predict every potential scenario.Feeling the data center heat The public's souring position on data centers poses a major risk for Anthropic, which relies on an ever-expanding portfolio of state-of-the-art computing facilities to train and maintain its prized foundation models.And with the midterm elections approaching, the tech industry's massive data center build-out has turned political, with lawmakers in 16 states considering moratoriums, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures."Opposition to data center development  has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," the filing said.Power problemsAnthropic's future success depends not only on building giant data centers, but also on the electrical and related power infrastructure needed to juice those computing facilities.The lack of "sufficient electrical power" across the nation and world poses big risks to Anthropic and its rivals, the filing notes. Even if energy becomes more readily available through "on-site natural gas-fired generation," that power could become more expensive with so much demand, the filing said.The kids are not alrightRivals like OpenAI and Meta have come under fire from lawmakers and plaintiffs' attorneys over allegations that the design and implementation of their AI models and apps have fostered certain child safety-related harms. Meta recently agreed to pay roughly $17 billion in a settlement with multiple state attorneys general in litigation involving child mental health and technology addiction.Thus far, Anthropic has largely avoided scrutiny, but the filing noted that the company could potentially face its own legal headaches. Based on its terms of service, minors aren't allowed to access Claude and related products.Anthropic knows it has work to do protecting children "as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access."No slowpokesThe company calling to pace the frontier also says it's a risk to move too slowly. Anthropic needs to keep racing and needs the rest of the business world to keep up. If companies curb their AI spending, Anthropic could feel the burn. "If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected," the filing says.The prospectus also cites reduced demand for frontier models as a risk. Customers might find that lower-cost models work fine for them and that "incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify the additional cost," instead choosing cheaper, or open-source alternatives.WATCH: Anthropic IPO filing shows what's happening on demand side of AI trade.watch now

title: Judge blasts prosecutors, refuses to sign new criminal complaint against ex-FBI officials
description: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Wash
body: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, Oct. 22, 2019.Susan Walsh | APA judge on Tuesday sharply criticized federal prosecutors for failing to get judicial approval before filing a new criminal complaint against two ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about investigations of Hunter Biden.Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said he would not sign off on the new complaint, which added a charge of obstruction against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C."I am not going to bless it as a superseding complaint," Faruqui said at a court hearing.He told prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, a judge would have to make a finding of probable cause that a crime had been committed by the defendants first, as opposed to sending him the complaint in the middle of the night, and expecting him to sign off on it.The judge said he did not believe that federal prosecutors had ever previously sought to file a criminal complaint without a judge's signature."I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"The superseding complaint that prosecutors in the office of D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro filed early Tuesday in court contained a signature block with Faruqui's name typed out. But the judge had not personally signed above his name.The filing came hours before prosecutors and lawyers for Floris and Benavides were scheduled to appear before Faruqui for a preliminary hearing on the original criminal complaint, unsealed last Friday, which accuses them of making false statements to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 about their involvement in investigations of Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden. Floris and Benavides were arrested Friday and have been released.The new superseding complaint sought to charge them with obstruction and attempted obstruction of a congressional proceeding.Floris' lawyers quickly filed a motion asking Faruqui to strike the superseding complaint, arguing it is legally deficient and filed in bad faith.Typically, criminal cases for conduct that occurred well in the past, as this one alleges, are lodged through a grand jury indictment. A criminal complaint, which does not require a grand jury's approval and can therefore be filed much faster, is often used to establish probable cause to get an arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly."In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," Floris' lawyers wrote in an emailed statement to CNBC on Tuesday morning."In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed. That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself," they wrote. "Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom," they said."We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing," Floris' legal team wrote.In their motion to strike the superseding criminal complaint, the lawyers argued that the document "represents a serious abuse of the criminal charging process, a troubling disregard for the judicial safeguards governing the initiation of criminal proceedings, and a calculated effort to evade judicial scrutiny and shield the government's allegations from adversarial testing at the scheduled preliminary hearing."

schema.headline: Judge blasts prosecutors, refuses to sign new criminal complaint against ex-FBI officials
